2 Celebrating the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence throughout 2026 is something Ada County is proud to be a part of. Next time you’re inside the Ada County Courthouse on Front Street in downtown Boise, you’ll notice two large banners hanging in the lobby. These banners serve as a reminder to all who pass through the courthouse of the significance of this seminal document. If you haven’t read the Declaration of Independence, it takes just five minutes and is an inspiring reminder of the brilliant vision our founders had. The Declaration of Independence

# Page 3^page=3
3 Each month we are featuring essays from Ada County leaders on what the Declaration of Independence means to them personally. If you’d like to read previous essays check out our newsletter archive Read more Ada County leadership essays Last month, I had the honor of attending National Police Week in Washington, D.C. While this is always a meaningful and solemn time, experiencing it during the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence made it especially impactful. The opportunity to walk through our nation’s monuments and museums---to reflect on what our country has endured, accomplished, and learned over the past 250 years---was nothing short of inspiring. Standing in the National Archives and reading the original Charters of Freedom---the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights---seeing the Star-Spangled Banner at the Museum of American History, walking the halls of the United States Capitol, and visiting the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum all served as powerful reminders of democracy, sacrifice, patriotism, and the responsibilities that come with authority. The Holocaust Memorial Museum, in particular, offered a sobering reminder of what can happen when authority is separated from humility, accountability, and respect for human dignity. As I stood in the National Archives Rotunda reading the original Declaration of Independence, I was reminded that true leadership is not defined by authority alone, but by service. In America, power belongs to the people, and those entrusted with authority have a responsibility to exercise it with humility, fairness, and respect. My badge and elected office give me authority, but public trust is earned through daily actions. It is often the small interactions that matter most. Our community judges public servants not by titles, but by integrity, honesty, fairness, and professionalism. Service also means protecting the rights of others---even when doing so is difficult. As public servants, we must remain professional in the face of criticism and confrontation, treat every person with dignity and respect, and recognize that restraint is often a sign of strength, not weakness. As an elected official, I am constantly reminded that my position---especially as the chief law enforcement officer of the county---is not ownership of power. It is a temporary stewardship entrusted to me by the people. Walking the streets of Washington, D.C., I found myself thinking about the generations of men and women who came before us and helped build this nation on enduring principles of liberty, equality, and self-government. America works best when those entrusted with authority never forget that they are first called to serve. That principle of service shaped our nation’s founding and remains essential to preserving liberty today. In my profession, I wear authority quite literally in the form of a badge. But the Declaration of Independence serves as a powerful reminder that authority alone is never the highest calling: service is.

4 SCENES FROM ADA COUNTY’S PARK AT EXPO IDAHO Coming in Late October It’s one of the biggest and most exciting events in our region in decades. Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho Opens October 23, 2026. This once-in-a- generation park nestled alongside the Boise River behind Ada County’s Expo Idaho will be a regional destination park. Each month, we share progress pictures as the park takes shape. The areas you see in these photos will look different a day later - that’s how rapidly the transformation is happening. Want to see updates on the all-wheel skate area, nature playground, restored wetlands, and more? Make sure you’re following Ada County on Facebook. https://www.facebook.com/AdaCountyIdaho/

6 ADA COUNTY GOVERNMENT In addition to elected offices, Ada County government includes twelve individual departments. Each department provides important services to our residents in Star, Eagle, Meridian, Boise, Garden City, Kuna, and Unincorporated Ada County. These services include law enforcement protection, emergency preparedness, election services, parks & waterways, indigent services, juvenile services, solid waste management, the Western Idaho Fair, Weed, Pest & Mosquito Abatement and more. Learn more about the services provided to you by Ada County - www.adacounty.id.gov/

8 KIMBERLY EASTMAN - 25 YEARS Kimberly started her Ada County career on May 7, 2001—and over the past 25 years in the Clerk’s Office, she’s done a little bit of everything (and then some). She started in Traffic Court on Barrister, where she processed judgments, answered calls from the public, and prepared workloads for all the judges. Fast forward to today, where she serves in the lead role for the criminal support staff. If there’s a task on the criminal support team, chances are she’s mastered it—and probably helped someone else learn it too. Kimberly’s service and dedication to Ada County is something to be admired. Thank you, Kimberly, for your service. Every year the Idaho Association of Counties awards scholarships to children of county employees to help offset the rising cost of college tuition. Seven scholarships are awarded annually, with one recipient selected from each district. This year’s recipient for Ada County is Clio Lindke, the daughter of Christian Lindke, a Research Analyst for Ada County Juvenile Services. This fall, Clio will attend Boise State University, where she plans to study Mechanical Engineering. Congratulations, Clio, and best of luck with all your future endeavors! The Idaho Association of Counties is a nonpartisan, nonprofit service organization that represents and supports all 44 of Idaho’s county governments Pictured L-R: Nora Lindke, Clio’s Sister; Jody Lindke, Clio’s mom; Christian Lindke, Clio’s Dad; Ada County Commission Board Chairman Rod Beck, Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley and Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson

9 Ada County Procurement procured an outstanding intern. Madison Hoglund is a May 2026 Boise State graduate who majored in Business Administration with a minor in Human Resources. “I grew up in a family dedicated to public service, with many relatives working for government as law enforcement. This internship is important to me because it allowed me to combine the values I learned growing up, that is community, ethics, and law, with my passion for business. This experience has given me the opportunity to learn from experienced professionals while gaining a deeper understanding of both government processes and the many functions of business. My knowledge of procurement has grown immensely, along with my skills in communication and professionalism.” Madison Hoglund Thank you to AC Boise for hosting the May 18th meeting of the Treasure Valley Partnership at the beautiful AC Boise soccer pitch. Thank you to the Treasure Valley mayors and community leaders who attended. Treasure Valley Partnership is a coalition of the Mayors and County Commissioners from Idaho’s Greater Treasure Valley. treasurevalleypartnership.org/
